metadata.XMP-dc:Description: Eine als Batman verkleidete Person steht vor einer brennenden Mülltonne. Demonstranten haben die Scheiben von Geschäften eingeschlagen, um diese zu plündern. In der Frankfurter Innenstadt haben sich Randalierer und Polizei am Abend Auseinandersetzungen geliefert. Gewalttäter schlugen Schaufensterscheiben von Geschäften ein, betroffen ist auch ein Waffengeschäft. Auch nach Auflösung einer Demonstration wegen wiederholter Attacken gegen Einsatzkräfte sind nach Darstellung der Polizei weiterhin gewalttätige Gruppen in der Frankfurter Innenstadt unterwegs. metadata.IFD0:ImageDescription:
An M23 member stands guard near a private residence damaged by a drone strike in Goma on March 11, 2026. Air strikes overnight Tuesday to Wednesday killed several people in the key eastern Democratic Republic of Congo city of Goma, controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 militia, sources told AFP.
Since taking up arms again in 2021, the M23 has seized swathes of the mineral-rich Congolese east with Rwanda's backing, unleashing a fresh spiral of violence in a region long plagued by fighting. 
Despite Rwanda and the DRC signing a peace deal at US President Donald Trump's urging in early December, in the latest attempt to end the conflict, clashes have continued at the front. (Photo by Jospin Mwisha / AFP)

npr.title: Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!

metadata.IFD0:ImageDescription:
An old LNG carrier in the final stage of disassembly for scrap metal on the mudflats of the Bay of Bengal, just north of Chattogram, Bangladesh. Breaking a ship like this will take about a year, with a crew of 60 men using blow torches and winches to drag the larger pieces ashore for cutting into smaller pieces. The nearby BSRM smelter melts down the scrap metal from the old boats and produces rebar and rolled steel, while the more valuable non-ferrous metals are sold overseas.  The brass from this ship was sold to Hyundai, the ship’s manufacturer in Korea, for use in new ships. From this LNG ship, they will collect a total of 30k tons of metal, plus 2.4k tons of aluminum and 200-300 tons of brass, copper, and stainless steel.  Bangladesh has no iron mines and relies on shipbreaking for much of its iron and steel.

Shipbreaking requires low wages and high demand for scrap steel.  LNG boats are more valuable as they have large quantities of non-ferrous metals that fetch higher prices.  

Bangladesh had 160 shipbreaking yards before the June 2025 regulation requiring that all new ship purchases after that date be broken using “green methods” requiring international certifications.  This forced most of the shipbreakers out of business, and now there are only 10 active shipbreaking yards.  The green regulations require a US$4-5 million investment in a thick concrete slab for breaking work, a crane, and toxic liquid storage tanks, as well as higher wages and international certifications.  resulting in higher operating costs.  This LNG ship was purchased before the June 2025 green deadline.

An old LNG carrier in the final stage of disassembly for scrap metal on the mudflats of the Bay of Bengal, just north of Chattogram, Bangladesh. Breaking a ship like this will take about a year, with a crew of 60 men using blow torches and winches to drag the larger pieces ashore for cutting into smaller pieces. The nearby BSRM smelter melts down the scrap metal from the old boats and produces rebar and rolled steel, while the more valuable non-ferrous metals are sold overseas.  The brass from this ship was sold to Hyundai, the ship’s manufacturer in Korea, for use in new ships. From this LNG ship, they will collect a total of 30k tons of metal, plus 2.4k tons of aluminum and 200-300 tons of brass, copper, and stainless steel.  Bangladesh has no iron mines and relies on shipbreaking for much of its iron and steel.

Shipbreaking requires low wages and high demand for scrap steel.  LNG boats are more valuable as they have large quantities of non-ferrous metals that fetch higher prices.  

Bangladesh had 160 shipbreaking yards before the June 2025 regulation requiring that all new ship purchases after that date be broken using “green methods” requiring international certifications. The Elgin Marbles are considered stolen goods by Greece, and has regularly demanded their return, while the Acropolis Museum, which houses the remaining sculptures, keeps an empty space for them within its current display. The British museum counters this, claiming that the sculptures were legally acquired by Lord Elgin following an agreement with Ottoman leaders. The British Museum is a public museum dedicated to human history, art and culture located in the Bloomsbury area of London. It has a permanent collection of eight million works and is among the largest and most comprehensive collection, which documents the story of human culture from its beginnings to the present.
